name: The Buddha
role: Founder of Buddhism (teacher in the Ganges basin, c. 5th century BCE)
summary: The Buddha taught a path of ethical conduct and meditation aimed at ending suffering, and his political ideas survive only in later-compiled Pali suttas. These present an ideal ruler who governs by principle, supports the poor and avoids harsh punishment, reject birth-based caste superiority, and ask for non-killing and non-harm. They record no programme on most modern policy questions.

cut-welfare.rationale: DN 26 attributes the spread of poverty, theft and violence to a king who did not provide money to the penniless, and DN 5 has the king supply seed, capital and wages. The same passage shows people stealing after a king gave money, so the evidence is mixed. Late text.

traditional-family.rationale: DN 31 lists reciprocal duties of parents, children, husband and wife as keeping society safe, but does not call family structure the foundation of society.

gradual-change.rationale: DN 16 says the Vajjis prosper while they keep the ancient principles, honour elders and shrines and do not abolish existing decrees; he also rejected caste claims, so the evidence is mixed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: DN 26 and DN 5 describe righteous kings, with the crown passing to the crown prince, as good rulers and give them advice; the texts are late and the idealised king is not a description of any actual state.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Dhammapada says all tremble at the rod and bids one neither kill nor incite killing, and that hatred is never ended by hatred; DN 26 has the ideal king rule 'without rod or sword'. Reported teachings, compiled later.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred: Dhammapada 201 says victory breeds enmity and the defeated sleep badly, and the wheel-turning king rules without rod or sword; no sutta discusses war's effect on national character.

results-over-ideology.rationale: In the Kalama Sutta people are to adopt what they know leads to welfare and happiness; the passage is about ethical practice, not policy.

means-match-ends.rationale: Inferred: 'Hatred is never laid to rest by hate, it is laid to rest by love' ties the method of resolving conflict to the peace sought.

rule-by-example.rationale: DN 26 has the king ruling by principle and consulting the virtuous, with order following from just conduct and livelihoods rather than from punishment; DN 5 finds punishment ineffective.

reason-over-faith.rationale: In the Kalama Sutta he tells people not to go by tradition, scripture or authority, but also not to rely on logic or inference alone, and to test teachings by their results.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In MN 98, MN 93 and DN 27 he rejects the claim that birth makes brahmins superior and says worth lies in deeds; this denies rank by birth but does not say worth is equal or speak of legal rights.

consent-of-governed.rationale: DN 27 describes the first ruler as chosen by the beings who asked him to judge and punish, and paid by them; mythic account recorded later.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Dhammapada 129-132 forbids harming others with a stick for one's own happiness and the precepts forbid killing and stealing; the texts state this without exceptions for a goal.

priority-to-poor.rationale: DN 26 lists providing money to the penniless as part of the noble duty of the wheel-turning monarch; late text.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: DN 26 traces widespread poverty to the ruler's failure to provide for the penniless, not to numbers of people.

death-penalty.rationale: In DN 5 he says execution, imprisonment, confiscation or banishment is not the right way to end a plague of raiders and recommends economic support instead; in DN 26 beheading thieves only escalates violence; the Dhammapada says neither to kill nor to incite killing. The texts are secondhand.

sacred-ruler.rationale: DN 27 presents the first king as a chosen and paid judge, not a divine descendant.

character-from-environment.rationale: In DN 26 and DN 5 poverty leads people to steal and a king who secures livelihoods ends the raiding, treating crime as a product of circumstances; the same texts also stress personal intention in other places.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: DN 26 tells the king to rely on principle and to have it as his authority, and describes decline when a king rules by his own ideas.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He rejects the brahmins' claim to superior status by birth (MN 98, MN 93, DN 27); the texts do not address hereditary titles or legal privileges as such.

elective-rulers.rationale: DN 27 says the first aristocrat-king was chosen by the people and paid in rice, while DN 26 has kings handing the realm to their sons; the account is mythic and points both ways.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Dhammapada 129-132 says all creatures love life and happiness and fear the rod, and one should not harm them; DN 26 has the king protect beasts and birds.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The first precept forbids killing living creatures and AN 5.177 says a lay follower should not trade in living beings or meat, which excludes using animals for food even with minimal suffering.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: DN 31 sets duties on the better-off toward dependants (pay and nurse workers, give them time off), and DN 5 praises a generous king; secondhand and not framed as a duty of the wealthy as a class.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: He advised rulers on just government (DN 26, DN 5, DN 16) yet held that the highest life is renunciation, and DN 26 has the ideal kings go forth.

filial-duty.rationale: DN 31 says a child should support parents who supported them, do their duty for them and make offerings after their death.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Dhammapada 186-187 says even a rain of money would not satisfy sensual desire, which brings little gratification and much suffering, and 204 calls contentment the ultimate wealth.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: DN 27 explains kingship as arising from the people's election and mocks the brahmin claim of descent from the Divinity.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: DN 26 and DN 5 present a king's provision for the poor and for working people as what restores order, and private giving to ascetics is a separate duty; late texts.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: In AN 8.51 he first refuses and then permits women to go forth as nuns, saying they can attain awakening, but under eight principles that put nuns beneath monks; late and disputed.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: DN 31 has the husband honour his wife, not look down on her and relinquish authority to her, with defined duties on both sides; the text does not describe full sharing.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred: the Dhammapada and the first precept forbid killing without recording any exception for self-defence, though no sutta addresses self-defence directly.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Dhammapada 274 declares the eightfold path 'the path, there is no other' for purification of vision; he treats other teachings as not leading to the same end.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: In the Kalama Sutta he says not to go by oral transmission, lineage, testament or canonical authority.

simple-living.rationale: He praises contentment and moderation (Dhammapada) and a renunciant life with few needs, but allowed lay followers to earn and keep wealth, so the answer is mixed.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Inferred: from the unqualified Dhammapada instruction not to kill or incite killing and the first precept, killing anyone without trial is not allowed.

notes: All sutta reports are secondhand and compiled centuries after his lifetime (DN 26 and DN 27 are often regarded as later), so no answer is high confidence. Answers are drawn only from the Pali Canon in Sujato's translation. The Dhammapada is a later verse anthology of sayings. Topics such as drug law, sex work, abortion, taxation, healthcare and the political system were not recorded as positions and are null, even though lay precepts (no intoxicants, no sexual misconduct) and AN 5.177 (no trade in weapons, beings, meat, intoxicants, poison) address personal conduct.
